title: Hate Speech Detection with Generalizable Target-aware Fairness

problem.claim: Hate speech detection classifiers can become biased toward specific targeted groups, producing false positives or false negatives that impair perceived fairness in content moderation.

gap.claim: Existing fairness-aware hate speech detection methods generally assume a narrow, known, fixed set of target groups and therefore do not generalize well to newly emerging targets.

contributions.claim: GetFair is a method for fairly classifying posts containing diverse and unseen target groups during inference.
GetFair uses adversarially trained filter functions to reduce the classifier's spurious dependence on target-related features.
GetFair uses a hypernetwork to generate target-specific filter weights and semantic gap alignment to rectify filters for unseen targets.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe GetFair as a new method and identify its hypernetwork parameterization and semantic gap alignment scheme as innovative or novel.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on two benchmark hate speech detection datasets reportedly show advantageous out-of-sample-target performance for GetFair compared with baselines.

narrative_sequence.summary: Hate speech detection is presented as important for limiting the early dissemination of toxic online posts.
Target-group bias can produce harmful classification errors and undermine trust in content moderation fairness.
Existing fairness-aware methods are limited to known fixed targets and struggle with newly emerging groups.
GetFair combines adversarial filtering, hypernetwork-generated target-specific filters, and semantic alignment for unseen targets.
The authors report favorable performance on out-of-sample targets across two benchmark datasets.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the datasets, baselines, metrics, or numerical results.
The abstract does not describe the training procedure, model architecture beyond the filtering components, or computational costs.
The abstract does not establish independent verification, reproducibility, or performance across target types beyond the reported experiments.
